# Code Reusability and Scalability in Web Projects


[Emre Yasin Çolakoğlu](https://medium.com/@emreyc?source=post_page---byline--ab8ed39bc60d---------------------------------------)


6 min read


·


Aug 22, 2022


--


Making the code **accessible** , **reusable** and **scalable** in an **organized** fashion not only benefits your **current** project but also your **future** projects. You can easily **pick up** from where you left off, **bootstrap** new projects with ease, **decrease** code maintenance costs, have a **simpler** mental model and **onboard** new members more effectively. 📈


We recently **improved** how we tackled these concepts in **Kunduz** and we’d like to share our findings.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


## Problems


### Amount of projects


For a long time, as a **growing** startup, our motto was to “Move fast & break things” 💥. **Non-critical** bugs were not a show stopper. We were able to publish bug fixes quickly. That mentality is also reflected in the **number** of projects we created. Instead of having a **monolith** as a project for different **stakeholders** of our product, we **divided** and **conquered** . We created **separate mini websites** for our students, tutors, annotators, ML matchers, and our corporate identity. 📦


This allowed us to **iterate** fast and find **product-market fit** more quickly, but as the products and features **matured** , a more **integrated** experience was needed to provide **value** . And our way of working **didn’t** provide that. ⚠️


### Project tree complexity


While there are **opinionated** best practices about how to organize projects, libraries, components, and code in general, our main development tool, **React** , doesn’t really impose anything. You can have gigantic **mono-components** or thousands of **mini components** , use **context** api, **swr** or **mobx** variants for data & state management, **classes** , hooks, **typescript** , enzyme or **testing library** etc. anything.


And having that many **aspects** of a feature in the same place increases the number of files in the project **tree** . It increases the **cognitive workload** of the developers. It causes **mistakes** . It **slows the onboarding** process of new hires. It creates **configuration problems** between tools. ⚙️


### Code complexity


Remember when I said React doesn’t empose anything? We took full advantage of that. We had components that retrieved its **own** **data** , displayed its own **skeleton UI** , implemented its own **business logic** , had its own **analytics codes** , and had **specific styles** for a **specific position** on the page its being used. 🎨


While it created some **beautifully outrageous** components & libraries and increased the development pace **spectacularly** , it never fully allowed us to **reuse** that component. This brings us to:


### Code Reusability


Well, what did we learn about **functions** in college?
“A function is simply a “chunk” of code that you can use over and over again, rather than writing it out **multiple** times.”


It’s like that but on a **whole project** level. Development time is a **finite** resource. We need to be **smart** about **what** code we write or **how** we write it to keep up with the sprint **timeline** , decrease the amount of code to **maintain,** or just increase the **efficiency** . 📦


We had **multiple** projects with **separate** git repositories. Some of them depended on the **same designs** . Some of them had **identical** features (auth). Some of them needed to access other project **resources** .


## Failed Attempts — Monorepo


Monorepos are awesome. You can have multiple projects in the same repository and access any of them anytime. Or so we thought.


If you dive into a monorepo setup **head-first** without thinking about how to **organize** your code in a shareable fashion, you are going to have a **bad time** .


By the time we first tested our monorepo solution, we had already merged different **mini projects** into a **monolith** . So we only had one deployable “ **app** ”. This made potential problems harder to find. When our one app was **working** fine, we thought *“this is it, we freakin’ did it”* . We didn’t have any reason to think **otherwise** . 😇


These all came crumbling down when I **introduced** another app to our monorepo. There were many problems with **importing** shared code, teaching **typescript** compiler the correct file paths, making sure **testing** and **ui tools** play nice with new setup, building the **correct** project, and not breaking our **existing** project in the process. 😈


There was something wrong with our solution. There had to be a better way to do this. Someone out there must have figured out how to do this better than we did.


And they did!


## Introducing: NX


By their definition, **Nx** is “Next generation build system with first-class monorepo support and powerful integrations.” This definition doesn’t do the tool justice. Nx **completely** abstracts the configuration phase of a monorepo. Things just work. Creating **workspaces** , **projects** , **libraries** , and **components** is a breeze. You have total control and freedom. 🏳


The official Nx plugin ecosystem is quite large and includes the best in the business. **React** , **React Native** , **Next.js** , **Storybook** , **Cypress** , **Node** , **Express** and more. They seamlessly work with each other and are contained in a single package.json file. No more “My newly created UI library uses React 18 but my legacy app has 17” problems. **Unit** and **e2e** testing infrastructure is created for you. No more “yeah, we didn’t have any time to write tests in this sprint” as an excuse. It’s right there. They magically work well together.


But enough promotion, let's talk shop;


To create a new workspace with nx, just run


```text
npx create-nx-workspace@latest
```


It will ask you for a **preset** , and some options as well. If you have something **specific** in mind, you can also run


```text
# create an empty workspace set up for building applications  npx create-nx-workspace --preset=apps   # create an empty workspace set up for building packages  npx create-nx-workspace --preset=core   # create an empty workspace set up for building packages with the @nrwl/js plugin installed  npx create-nx-workspace --preset=ts
```


The folder structure is like below, and I must say it's pretty much **standard** at this point. What makes Nx special is you can give **tags** to your individual projects and decide who can depend on whom.[See here](https://nx.dev/structure/monorepo-tags)


```text
myorg/  ├── apps/  ├── libs/  ├── tools/  ├── workspace.json  ├── nx.json  ├── package.json  └── tsconfig.base.json
```


Another **useful** trick is the -affected option. With this, Nx only runs tests on **changed** code.


```text
nx affected --target=test
```


This will tell Nx to figure out what changed, what those **changes** depend on, and only run tests on affected areas. This **saves** development and CI time.


Nx supports many **tools** & **technologies** . You can go pretty far with the official packages[listed here](https://nx.dev/packages) or[you can check out the community plugins](https://nx.dev/community#plugin-directory)


[Reference: Official Packages & API Reference: Official Packages & API Reference: Official Packages & APInx.dev](https://nx.dev/packages?source=post_page-----ab8ed39bc60d---------------------------------------)


One of its most advertised features is its **cache** system. With this, Nx promises it never runs the **same** computation **twice** . If you didn’t change your code and tried to build again, it’s near **instant** . This feature is not limited to build outputs though. It supports **test results** as well. Combined with the -affected option, Nx helps developers and projects save time. 💪


We recently migrated our monorepo codebase to Nx and started to refactor our features under` /libs/feature-*` packages. It will allow us to share code more effectively and contain related business logic in the same space. While doing that, all the data access infrastructure got moved under` /libs/data-access-*` packages and all shared ui code got moved under` /libs/ui-*` packages.


For example, with the development of[Next.js Layout RFC](https://nextjs.org/blog/layouts-rfc) the layout structure of a typical Next.js project will change and pages will have special logics. **Migrating** our features to bite-sized individual **packages** will allow us to do required Next.js changes without moving many files around. And that will lead to **fewer bugs** , mistakes, and effort all around.


We really liked what this tool offered and hope to have a scalable and accessible project structure for many years to come.
